{"id": "42:36/q13", "question": "What do على and the imperfect verb add to the portrayal of reliance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "42:36/q13/p1", "position": "على pictures placing a burden on God, while the imperfect depicts reliance renewed with each concern.", "reasons": "Biqa'i says this imagery conveys ease and freedom from worry."}]}
{"id": "42:36/q14", "question": "What occasion of revelation is reported?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "42:36/q14/p1", "position": "Abu Bakr gave away all his wealth for God, was reproached, and the verse was revealed.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi, and Elmalili attribute the report to Ali; Abu Hayyan and Alusi say both Muslims and disbelievers criticized him, whereas Bursevi says all Muslims and other reports say people or a group. Qurtubi adds a hadith saying he spent eighty thousand. Alusi states no grading."}]}
{"id": "42:36/q15", "question": "What example is told of leaving worldly attachment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "42:36/q15/p1", "position": "Harun al-Rashid's young son chose ascetic worship and left worldly status behind.", "reasons": "Bursevi says the sixteen-year-old son's bird obeyed him but not Harun, and the son said his father's worldliness shamed him before God's friends. Abu Amir al-Wa'iz al-Basri says the prince departed with a ring and Quran, earned a dirham and daniq by Saturday labor in Basra, worked tenfold when hired, and was later found ill in a ruin."}]}
{"id": "42:36/q16", "question": "What conduct does the contrast between worldly goods and God's reward urge?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "42:36/q16/p1", "position": "Give worldly goods their limited place, pursue God's enduring reward through faith, reliance, obedience, and detachment.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says the verse diminishes worldly life and urges lasting blessings and high rank. Jishumi reports an exhortation to work for God rather than worldly gain. Ibn Kathir says not to choose the perishing and mentions patiently leaving pleasures. Bursevi says to consider the outcome from the outset, cites a Persian maxim, and calls the choice God's gift to whom He wills. Ibn Ashur says worldly safety or wealth should not be a final goal. Kuran Yolu calls means divine gifts; Islahi says believers should desire the future reward."}]}
{"id": "42:36/q17", "question": "How does verse 36 follow the preceding passage?", "turns_on": "Which preceding theme chiefly supplies the transition: changing blessings, provision and sea danger, or affliction and patience.", "positions": [{"id": "42:36/q17/p1", "position": "The signs of rain and creatures show worldly blessings can disappear and change, preparing the contrast with lasting good.", "reasons": "Biqa'i draws the transition from the preceding natural signs."}, {"id": "42:36/q17/p2", "position": "It extends the earlier discussion of expanded and restricted provision and of God's pardon amid sea-voyage danger.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur traces it to 42:27 and 42:34, and includes safety at sea among passing worldly goods."}, {"id": "42:36/q17/p3", "position": "It sits in the sūra's treatment of affliction, patience, and adversity under God's will.", "reasons": "Samarrai links the surrounding passages at 42:30, 42:43, and 42:48 to the contrast between passing provision and lasting good."}]}
{"id": "42:36/q18", "question": "How do later passages develop this contrast?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "42:36/q18/p1", "position": "They describe believers' qualities and wrongdoers' fate, then return to the contrast of temporary worldly life and lasting reward.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i says the verse divides provision between worldly gifts shared by believers and unbelievers and afterlife reward for believers before listing virtues and wrongdoers' fate. Islahi says 42:44–50 resumes this contrast, giving oppressed Muslims immediate glad tidings and foreshadowing their success."}]}
{"id": "42:36/q19", "question": "Why does the parallel in al-Qasas mention adornment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "42:36/q19/p1", "position": "Al-Qasas contains Qarun's public display of adornment, while al-Shura contains no comparable worldly scene.", "reasons": "Samarrai relates the added word to 28:79; he also reports Ma'tarak al-aqran making the same contextual connection."}]}
{"id": "42:36/q20", "question": "What broader themes of the sūra are connected with this verse and its believers' qualities?", "turns_on": "The notes connect the passage with different overarching themes: two harvests, faith embodied in conduct, or communal consultation.", "positions": [{"id": "42:36/q20/p1", "position": "The sūra contrasts people pursuing this world's harvest with those seeking the Hereafter's harvest.", "reasons": "Study Quran states this as a theme of the sūra."}, {"id": "42:36/q20/p2", "position": "Faith must become conduct that reshapes individual and communal life, including duties to God and relations with others.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu says the Quran aims to transform the Jahiliyya order and form an exemplary generation; Elmalili calls faith and reliance foundational to religious and communal success."}, {"id": "42:36/q20/p3", "position": "Consultation among believers is a basic principle of their community and gives the sūra its title.", "reasons": "Asad's introduction notes the title from consultation among believers in this passage."}]}
{"id": "42:36/q21", "question": "How is the following verse's expression for major sin or sins read?", "turns_on": "Whether the reading uses a collective singular or an explicit plural; Tabrisi supplies linguistic and Quranic support for each.", "positions": [{"id": "42:36/q21/p1", "position": "Kufan readers except Asim use the singular, which can have collective sense.", "reasons": "Tabrisi reports the singular here and in al-Najm; he says singular wording can denote a collective, comparing Quranic references to God's blessing and Arabic usage, with 16:18."}, {"id": "42:36/q21/p2", "position": "The remaining readers use the plural, supported by the Quranic phrase major sins.", "reasons": "Tabrisi reports this reading here and in al-Najm and cites 4:31 in support."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q01", "question": "Who is addressed as the potential questioner?", "turns_on": "Whether the surrounding consolation fixes a particular addressee or the conditional address is general.", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q01/p1", "position": "The Prophet Muhammad.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr relates this to the passage's consolatory address to him."}, {"id": "43:9/q01/p2", "position": "Any potential questioner.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr also allows the address to be general."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q02", "question": "Who are the people denoted by 'them' and 'they'?", "turns_on": "The antecedent of the plural pronouns: the nearer unbelievers or the prophets.", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q02/p1", "position": "The Meccan or Arab polytheists, especially Quraysh.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī prefers the nearer antecedent, the unbelievers, while acknowledging a possible prophetic referent. Muqātil, Ibn ʿAbbās as reported by al-Wāḥidī, and many commentators identify Muhammad's people; al-Biqāʿī says Quraysh knew the earlier peoples' histories."}, {"id": "43:9/q02/p2", "position": "The prophets.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī mentions the possibility but favors the nearer unbelieving antecedent. Some commentators reported by Study Quran take the following verses 43:10–13 as potentially continuing the prophets' answer."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q03", "question": "How does this question connect to the preceding passage?", "turns_on": "The notes point to different contextual connections: an interrupted address, earlier peoples, or the monotheistic argument after 43:6.", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q03/p1", "position": "It resumes the preceding address after an interruption about earlier messengers.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the verses beginning 'How many messengers We sent' (43:6) interrupt to affirm the point and console the Prophet."}, {"id": "43:9/q03/p2", "position": "It builds on Quraysh's knowledge of earlier peoples.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says Quraysh heard their histories and would admit what they knew; God had made them generally truthful, preparing their admission about creation."}, {"id": "43:9/q03/p3", "position": "It turns the passage into an argument for God's oneness against the Meccans.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr relates it to the promise of victory in 43:6 and the contradiction of rejecting the Messenger's call to one God while admitting God created all worlds; their admission implicitly denies idols a right to worship."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q04", "question": "What is the force of the emphatic conditional wording?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q04/p1", "position": "It makes their answer certain while dramatizing their incoherence.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites the prefatory oath lām, the answer lām, and the emphatic nūn; treating an undisputed fact as debatable heightens the contradiction."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q05", "question": "Why is their admission elicited through a staged question?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q05/p1", "position": "A direct question exposes a truth they disregard in conduct and prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says they immediately answer Allah when asked, then return to association of partners."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q06", "question": "What does مَّنْ mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q06/p1", "position": "It is the interrogative 'who'.", "reasons": "Bursevī explicitly glosses the interrogative."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q07", "question": "What do the heavens and earth denote here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q07/p1", "position": "The upper and lower cosmic bodies.", "reasons": "Bursevī supplies this description of the two terms."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q08", "question": "What does creating the heavens and earth mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q08/p1", "position"

{"id": "43:9/q09", "question": "Why does the verse state creation explicitly?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q09/p1", "position": "The opponents appeared to deny origination, so their claim needed an explicit creation statement.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān describes them as apparently materialists or deniers for whom the heavens' creation had to be said outright."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q10", "question": "Why is خَلَقَهُنَّ repeated in the answer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q10/p1", "position": "It stresses the admission and answers the question in meaning, though a syntactically matching answer would be nominal.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says repetition intensifies emphasis and notes that مَّنْ is a subject, so literal syntactic correspondence would require a nominal answer. Al-Samīn illustrates that 'Who stood?' could be answered merely 'Zayd.' Al-Biqāʿī says the direct answer Allah would suffice, but repetition strengthens the rebuke. Al-Ālūsī follows Abū Ḥayyān's distinction between semantic and grammatical matching."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q11", "question": "How can a short 'Allah' answer to a creator question be supplied grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q11/p1", "position": "An omitted predicate can be understood from the explicit question.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān gives questions about who created heaven and earth or sent rain, with 'Allah' as the answer."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q12", "question": "What does this answer show about the word Allah in 43:87?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q12/p1", "position": "Allah is the agent of an understood verb, not a predicate starting a subjectless sentence.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says the explicit verb here confirms nominative Allah as agent in 43:87 rather than an initial subject. Al-Itqān rejects the subjectless-predicate analysis on the strength of this parallel."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q13", "question": "Whom do the respondents acknowledge as creator?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q13/p1", "position": "God alone, the mighty and knowing Creator.", "reasons": "Muqātil calls Him mighty in dominion and knowing of creation; al-Ṭabarī says mighty in power and vengeance and knowing all within creation. Ibn ʿAbbās, as reported by al-Wāḥidī, says the people thereby affirm His justice and knowledge. Al-Ṭabrisī adds His knowledge of creatures' interests. Abū Ḥayyān observes that elsewhere their answer uses Allah, the comprehensive name for the supreme attributes. Ibn ʿĀshūr compares their answer in Luqmān 31:25; Study Quran cites 10:31, 23:84–85, 29:61, 29:63, 31:25, 39:38, and 43:87."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q14", "question": "Did the respondents themselves say 'the Mighty, the Knowing'?", "turns_on": "Whether the titles are the speakers' own words, implicit in their acknowledgment, or part of the Qur'an's expanded presentation.", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q14/p1", "position": "Yes, these titles can be their actual words.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī offers this reading. Abū Ḥayyān holds that their own wording may be these titles despite other verses giving 'Allah.' Bursevī reports it as another possibility. Ibn al-Munīr, reported by al-Ālūsī, parses the titles as their answer; al-Ālūsī prefers that as more apparent from the wording."}, {"id": "43:9/q14/p2", "position": "The titles convey the truth of their attribution to God without requiring that they uttered them.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī says the attributes may be implicit in the content of their answer, effectively 'God.' Al-Irshād, reported by Bursevī, and al-Zamakhsharī, reported by al-Ālūsī, say they ascribe creation to the One who truly has these attributes without necessarily using or consciously describing Him by these titles; al-Ālūsī accepts this as sufficient. Elmalılı says admission of creation entails these and other divine attributes. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the Meccans actually said Allah as in 31:25, and would also affirm that He is mighty and knowing if asked."}, {"id": "43:9/q14/p3", "position": "The Qur'an gives an expanded divine formulation beyond an expected simple 'God' answer.", "reasons": "Fath al-Raḥmān, reported by Bursevī, says the expected answer was that God created them and the Qur'anic wording introduces God's following attributes, distinct from the reported answer."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q15", "question": "Where does the reported answer end?", "turns_on": "Whether the answerers are the idolaters or prophets, and how the change to divine first-person speech is understood.", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q15/p1", "position": "It ends by the divine titles, and the following description is God's speech.", "reasons": "The author of al-Naẓm, reported by al-Wāḥidī, points to the shift from the unbelievers' answer to 'for you' rather than their expected 'for us'; the attributes still name the same God. Al-Wāḥidī and al-Zamakhsharī say God's own description follows the answer. Al-Bayḍāwī proposes a new sentence after the actual answer. Abū Ḥātim, reported by al-Nasafī, normally keeps alladhī connected to al-ʿAlīm, but allows a pause by supplying huwa. Ibn al-Munīr and al-Ālūsī place God's continuation after the titles; al-Ālūsī finds 'We brought forth' in verse 11 natural after a speaker shift and compares Moses' speech followed by 'We brought forth' in 20:52–53. Elmalılı points to the third-to-first-person shift in the revival statement."}, {"id": "43:9/q15/p2", "position": "On a prophetic referent, verses 43:10–13 may continue the answerers' quotation.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this possibility from some commentators."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q16", "question": "What does 'the Mighty' signify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q16/p1", "position": "God has overwhelming, unconquerable power and dominion.", "reasons": "Muqātil stresses dominion; al-Ṭabarī adds power and vengeance. Al-Rāzī derives perfect power from the capacity to overpower. Al-Biqāʿī says He overcomes everything and nothing overcomes Him. Al-Ṭabrisī says He is almighty."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q17", "question": "What does 'the Knowing' signify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q17/p1", "position": "God's knowledge is complete and encompasses creation.", "reasons": "Muqātil says He knows His creation; al-Ṭabarī says He knows them and everything within heaven and earth. Al-Ṭabrisī adds that He knows creatures' interests. Al-Rāzī calls it perfect knowledge; al-Biqāʿī says it encompasses all things."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q18", "question": "Why are might and knowledge highlighted together?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q18/p1", "position": "They display the Creator's power and knowledge against the idols' helplessness.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says complete knowledge and power make creation of every possible thing possible, before the passage details God's works. Al-Biqāʿī says the names entail unconquerable power and comprehensive knowledge. Elmalılı says their admission entails these and earlier attributes. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the names embarrass those who turn to weak, ignorant idols, which cannot even protect themselves from human hands. Kur'an Yolu says the idolaters never treated idols as God's equals in every quality and knew creation requires great power and knowledge."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q19", "question": "What proof of God is drawn from the world's creation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q19/p1", "position": "The world's origination and God's agency provide the first proof of God.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says theologians make this the first divine attribute and first proof, taking creation as bringing the world into being."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q20", "question": "What does their admission imply for worship and lordship?", "turns_on": "Whether the emphasis falls on exclusive worthiness of worship or on exclusive governance of needs.", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q20/p1", "position": "Only the Creator deserves worship; their idols and partners have no comparable claim.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī says they contradict their confession by worshiping idols. Al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Rāzī, and others expose the inconsistency. Ibn ʿĀshūr says idols are created stones and only the worshippers' Creator deserves worship. Al-Biqāʿī stresses the objects of worship lack power and knowledge and their own answer refutes their excuse. Ibn Kathīr says they nonetheless worship idols and rivals. Study Quran cites parallel admissions in 10:31, 23:84–85, 29:61, 29:63, 31:25, 39:38, and 43:87."}, {"id": "43:9/q20/p2", "position": "God's creative acts also establish His sole governance of human needs.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says 43:9–14 argue that God alone is Lord because His acts of creation govern human needs; the polytheists nonetheless assign governance to others."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q21", "question": "What does this confession imply about resurrection?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q21/p1", "position": "Denial of resurrection contradicts acknowledgment of God's creative power.", "reasons": "The scholars of meaning reported by al-Wāḥidī call this extreme ignorance. Al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, and al-Rāzī say they deny His power to resurrect while admitting His creation. Study Quran reports the same denial and cites other confession passages. Islāḥī says cosmic signs support both divine oneness and the Day of Judgement."}]}

Al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī, and Bursevī likewise call it ignorance; Ibn ʿĀshūr says they disregard the Creator in life and prayer and immediately return to shirk after answering."}, {"id": "43:9/q23/p2", "position": "Their own admission reveals deliberate obstinacy.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says the idols have neither power nor knowledge, so the confession refutes the idolaters' excuse."}, {"id": "43:9/q23/p3", "position": "They treat idols as intermediaries who can bring benefit, avert harm, and draw them closer to God.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu cites 10:18 and 39:3 for this explanation."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q24", "question": "What grounds recognition of God's creative power in human beings?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q24/p1", "position": "Primordial covenantal testimony planted recognition of divine lordship and creation.", "reasons": "Bursevī says the covenant's affirmation bears fruit in worldly recognition of creative power, citing 7:172; only God's gracious attraction opens the way to His majesty."}]}
{"id": "43:9/q25", "question": "How does the argument continue in the following verses and the sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:9/q25/p1", "position": "It unfolds God's works to support exclusive lordship, resurrection, and the sūra's challenge to idolatry.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī says the next verse continues the rebuke (43:10). Al-Rāzī says the passage details the Creator's works after naming perfect power and knowledge. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says 43:9–14 joins creation to governance of human needs. Islāḥī says 43:9–15 joins cosmic signs to tawḥīd and the Day of Judgement and treats the whole sūra as a harmonious unit. Study Quran says the sūra answers Makkan objections and forms of disbelief."}]}
{"id": "43:10/q01", "question": "How is ٱلَّذِى construed grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the relative noun continues the preceding description of al-ʿazīz or begins a sentence with an understood huwa.", "positions": [{"id": "43:10/q01/p1", "position": "It is the predicate of an omitted subject, understood as 'He who made.'", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas gives an omitted subject as one possibility. Ibn Ashur supplies huwa alladhi and, following al-Sakkaki's terminology, says subject omission accords with established usage; the relative pronoun is known through its clause and functions like a proper name."}, {"id": "43:10/q01/p2", "position": "It is a nominative adjective of al-ʿazīz in the preceding verse.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas gives this as the other nominative analysis."}]}
{"id": "43:10/q02", "question": "Whose speech begins with ٱلَّذِى جَعَلَ لَكُمُ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:10/q02/p1", "position": "It begins God's own description after the report of the unbelievers' answer.", "reasons": "The author of al-Nazm, al-Razi, and al-Qurtubi note that unbelievers would have said 'for us,' whereas the verse says 'for you'; al-Razi adds that the later 'We revived' is divine speech and compares a listener adding praise of a mosque's builder after another speaker names him. Al-Wahidi says the new clause adds a true divine attribute to the one quoted from them; Ibn Atiyya calls it a fresh report; Abu Hayyan says it reminds people of earlier blessings; Bursevi calls it a fresh divine relative clause. Both speakers' descriptions concern the same God. Al-Qurtubi says the new declaration displays God's complete power."}]}
{"id": "43:10/q03", "question": "What is the force of directly addressing people and repeating لَكُمُ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:10/q03/p1", "position": "The address presses the rebuke and highlights God's benefits to people.", "reasons": "Al-Biqaʿi says the shift to direct address sharpens rebuke and recalls kindness that ought to bring submission. Al-Tabatabaʾi says it exposes the incoherence of admitting God alone creates while assigning governance elsewhere. Ibn Ashur says the two occurrences of lakum mark human benefit and distinguish this passage from 78:6–7, where vast creation argues for resurrection; he adds that the eleven second-person pronouns across four verses are expected address, not iltifat."}]}
{"id": "43:10/q04", "question": "What does making the earth مَهْدًۭا convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "43:10/q04/p1", "position": "God prepared the earth as a stable, comfortable, usable resting place for human life and movement.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls it a bed or floor; al-Tabari a spread bed to walk and tread on, citing 20:53, and reports al-Suddi's carpet; al-Mawardi a resting spread; al-Thaʿlabi a cradle; Ibn Atiyya a prepared spread for settling and movement; al-Razi cites stability, cultivation, construction, concealment of flaws of living and dead, and a child's cradle's comforts. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi stress rest and settlement; Ibn Kathir says people walk, stand, and sleep on it and that mountains fix it above flowing water against swaying. Al-Biqaʿi says it is firm and level though God could have made it quake or unstable on water. Bursevi defines mahd and mihad as prepared and smoothed, cites 2:22, and reports Bahr al-ʿUlum's sitting, sleeping, and turning in a bed. Al-Alusi says its immense size reconciles a leveled surface with a spherical body; Ibn Ashur says its flattened habitable surface is what benefits people here despite its spherical body, and cites 7:41. Al-Tabatabaʾi likens its nurturing to a child's cradle; Kuranyolu specifies walking, working, resting, and living; Study Quran reports ease of travel, agriculture, and habitation."}]}
{"id": "43:10/q05", "question": "How is the word مَهْدًۭا read?", "turns_on": "The transmitted readers and the presence or absence of the alif, with corresponding vowel patterns; the notes say the sense is shared.", "positions": [{"id": "43:10/q05/p1", "position": "Mahdan, without an alif after hāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid assigns this to ʿAsim, Hamza, and al-Kisaʾi in Ta Ha and al-Zukhruf; al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi call it the Kufan reading, and Ibn Atiyya also names Ibn Masʿud, Talha, and al-Aʿmash. Ibn al-Jazari specifies fatḥa on mīm and still hāʾ, and calls Ibn Mihran's report from Rawh erroneous. Al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur name ʿAsim; Ibn Ashur and Ibn Atiyya say its sense equals mihadan. Qiraat-ER presents mahdan as the form replaced by its variant."}, {"id": "43:10/q05/p2", "position": "Mihādan, with an alif after hāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid assigns this to Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir throughout the Qurʾan.
